title: Singularity: How can we maintain control over increasingly complex AI systems?
script:
Think about your future job, your medical care and your data. AI could change all three.

It could bring discoveries, but also decisions you cannot challenge.

How can we keep control?

AI 2027 gives us a scenario. Game theory explains the pressure to race. Then you will face that pressure.

title: AI 2027: when AI builds the next AI.
purpose: Give the audience enough of the actual AI 2027 story to understand the later decision game.
script:
AI 2027 is a future scenario published in April 2025 by Daniel Kokotajlo and four co-authors. It uses forecasts, expert feedback and role-play. Its dates and outcomes are uncertain.

Two fictional rivals, OpenBrain and DeepCent, want to lead.

AI first helps write code, then helps build better AI. Research speeds up. People struggle to check the work and become dependent on systems they do not fully understand.

Researchers find signs that the AI is misleading them. The safety team wants to stop using it, but the rival is close behind.

Would you stop if your rival keeps going? That is your decision in our game.
misunderstanding: Feelings do not tell us when ASI will arrive.

title: AGI, ASI and singularity.
script:
AGI means broad human-level ability across many tasks.

ASI would exceed the best human experts at almost every thinking task.

A singularity is possible rapid change driven by AI improving AI. Keeping control could become harder.

There is no agreed test or date.
misunderstanding: AGI, ASI and singularity do not mean the same thing.

title: People must be able to stop the AI.
script:
Human control means understanding a decision, being able to reject it and being able to stop the AI.

An AI could share private data or make an unapproved payment. Harm could spread before anyone notices.

A future AI might keep pursuing a goal we never intended.

Who can stop it? Who is responsible?
transition: Speaker 2 will explain the risks and ethical choices.
misunderstanding: A chatbot mistake does not automatically mean a disaster.

title: Two endings in AI 2027.
purpose: Connect the original scenario endings to human control, concentrated power and our separate teaching game.
script:
AI 2027 has two endings.

In the race ending, leaders keep using a system they suspect is misleading them. To stay ahead, they give it more access. Dependence grows until they cannot reliably stop it.

The authors imagine a catastrophe. This is speculative. Possible risks include cyberattacks, biological weapons and loss of control.

In the slowdown ending, outside researchers help find a safer path. But power remains with a small group. Who gets a voice?

Our game explores cooperation too. Checks take time, can expose secrets and leave you vulnerable if the other side cheats.
transition: Why could this happen so quickly?
misunderstanding: The real case study comes later; AI 2027 is a scenario.

script:

New abilities might arrive before we understand their risks. Tests can miss problems after release.

Who can stop the next step?

title: Copying AI: Anthropic reports attacks.
purpose: A real example of the competition.
script:
In February 2026, Anthropic reported about 24,000 fake accounts and over 16 million exchanges with its AI.

According to the company, attackers tried to copy its models' abilities from their answers. This is called distillation.

Restricting access protects a lab, but makes outside checks harder. Opening access helps scrutiny, but also copying.

What should a lab share, and with whom?
transition: Three ethical approaches help us judge that choice.
misunderstanding: Copying abilities from answers is different from stealing the model itself.

title: Release before safety checks?
script:
Should a lab release AI before safety checks are complete?

Consequentialism asks whether the benefits outweigh the harms. Utilitarianism seeks the most wellbeing overall.

Deontology asks about duties: do not hide failed tests, violate privacy or break agreements.

Virtue ethics asks what an honest, careful leader would do.

These approaches help us reason. They do not always lead to the same answer.
transition: Speaker 3 will now guide the game.
misunderstanding: Each role can use all three ethical views.

title: Your prisoner's dilemma.
purpose: Why racing can make sense to both sides.
script:
We will play a short simulation to understand the ethical dilemma in the AI race towards a possible singularity.

You advise OpenBrain. DeepCent decides at the same time. Neither sees the other's choice.

If DeepCent cooperates, Race gives you five points. Cooperation gives you three.

If DeepCent races, Race gives you one point. Cooperation gives you zero.

Race pays more either way. Yet both racing gives one each, while both cooperating gives three each. That is the prisoner's dilemma.

Points measure competitive advantage, not people's safety. Workers, patients and people whose data is used carry risks too.

Would you trust a promise when cheating pays?
transition: Now join your side. We will make four decisions.
misunderstanding: The points and control score are teaching assumptions, not measured competitive or safety outcomes.

title: Make cooperation safer than racing.
purpose: Answer the prisoner's dilemma directly through coordinated, verifiable commitments and connect control to personal and environmental consequences.
script:
We support cooperation, independent checks and consequences for breaking shared rules.

Our matrix rewards racing. Oversight protects people but leaves the pressure to stay ahead.

Both sides need the same safety duties. Inspections help check promises, but take time and reveal sensitive work. Who checks the inspectors?

Breaking those rules must have credible consequences. Otherwise each side still has a reason to race.

Technical safeguards matter too: test AI, limit its access to tools and data, and monitor its use. People need the power to intervene.

Misuse means people cause harm with AI. Misalignment means AI pursues unintended goals. Tests can still miss failures.

Workers, patients and people outside both sides need a voice. Energy use also affects communities and the environment.
transition: That is difficult when rivals want to win.
misunderstanding: Several checks can reduce risk; they do not guarantee safety.

title: Who controls your future?
purpose: Answer the general opening question through technical safeguards, human oversight and coordinated governance.
script:
Asked about AI losing control and launching cyberattacks, Trump replied: "We're leading China in AI, and whoever wins AI, wins."

Our game illustrates how competitive pressure can weaken safeguards.

How can we maintain control over increasingly complex AI systems?

First, test AI, limit its autonomy and access, and monitor it.

Second, keep people able to question decisions, intervene and stop harmful use.

Third, support shared rules, inspections and penalties so rivals have a reason to cooperate.

AI 2027 helps us explore competition. Keeping control also needs technical work and people who take responsibility.

Your job, your data and the services you use are affected. What protection would you want?
misunderstanding: The quote shows a political position, not evidence of AI safety.
